children: The Federal Reserve will potentially need more interest-rate hikes to bring inflation back to target than currently priced in by markets, Said Haidar, founder and chief investment officer of Haidar Capital Management, said.

The Fed raised the federal funds target rate range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00% last week and signaled another hike for this year. Money markets currently price in three 25-basis-point hikes over the next 12 months, according to LSEG.

"Despite only signaling one additional hike this year and none thereafter, the market reacted hawkishly to the Fed's dot plot [at the September meeting], in a sign of continued complacency about the need to tighten monetary policy," Haidar said.

While the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting could prove uncomfortably close to the midterm elections, Haidar Capital Management expects a minimum of two additional rate hikes in December 2026 and March 2027.
"However, we anticipate that at least four to six hikes will be required to have a significant effect on inflation."

By acknowledging rising geopolitical tensions and the resulting surge in energy prices as a factor in deciding to hike, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh seemingly abandoned the Fed's previous practice of looking through supply shocks due to its supposed inability to effect supply shock-driven inflation, Haidar said.

"Given that the worst episodes in the Fed's history--namely, the 1970s and the post-Covid 2021-2022 period--were characterized by large inflation overshoots resulting from the Fed's decision to look through supply shocks, it would be difficult to imagine the Fed continuing this practice," he said.
Warsh's explicit reference to "second and third order effects" resulting from the energy crisis seemingly conveyed an understanding of the need to take a different approach, he noted.

Speaking on the Treasury's increased buybacks of long-dated debt, Haidar said the move could keep long-end yields contained for now, but the approach subjects the U.S. to rapidly rising debt costs if short-term rates are raised by the Fed.

While the Treasury likely has additional capacity to try to hold down long-end bond yields, the bond market can ultimately overpower the relatively small arsenal at the Treasury's disposal--even as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dares the market to challenge him, he said.

"For now, however, Bessent has flattened the Treasury curve (aided as well by the Fed's hawkish pivot) and caused the 20-year [maturity] to richen versus on-the-run 10-year and 30-year [debt]," he said.

"But it is difficult to see this recent curve-flattening being sustained, as rising European debt supply to fund greater defense and infrastructure spending, outsized corporate debt issuance by hyper-scalers to finance AI investments, and significant fiscal expansion in Japan are all likely to push up global term premiums."
Haidar sees room for higher Treasury yields, expecting 10-year yields to land somewhere between 5.25% and 5.75% by year-end. They last traded at 4.934%.
"Elevated global bond supply coupled with strong corporate earnings worldwide make it likely that bond yields will have to rise," he said.
Haidar Capital Management had approximately $660 million of assets under management as at Aug. 31, 2026.
